quotes.text: Esau valued more highly what he had lost after it was gone, as many people do, and vowed violent revenge after the death of father Isaac. But the alert and resourceful Rebekah averted the double tragedy of loss of one son by murder and the other by the execution in accord with the law (Genesis 9:6); she proposed to Isaac that Jacob be sent away to find a proper wife in her ancestral homeland. Thus she would get Jacob away for "a few days" until Esau's anger cooled. He actually would be away for twenty years.

notes.text: What is it? The gateway into heaven. Isn't that a perfect description of the temple? 18 And Jacob rose up early in the morning, and took the stone that he had put for his pillows, and set it up for a pillar, and poured oil upon the top of it. 19 And he called the name of that place Beth-el; but the name of that city was called Luz at first. So he names the place, House of God, and sets up a rock or stone and anoints it. Don't picture the ladder as the one you have in your garage. The best representation of this ladder you can find in south or central America, being a pyramid with steps. What was at the top? The LORD. What was at the bottom of the ladder? Jacob. Who came up and down it with information? Angels. Anciently, this shape was a temple; particularly in Central America. What was always at the top of the long stairway? The House of their God. They always climbed up the "step-pyramid." Joseph Smith taught that Jacob's ladder was none other than the telestial, terrestrial and celestial kingdoms. This then is the same thing that happened to Abraham between the pieces of the carcass. The same covenants, the same story, just told differently. Now, something else happens. What did he put there to represent what he saw? He took a stone, and set it upright, and poured oil on it. This will help you understand apostasy in ancient Israel, and how they could eventually go over to the worship of Baal. Guess what represented Baal. None other than a stone standing on end. That's it. Often there was no chiseling, but just a stone stuck on its end. What did Jacob just do. Same thing, but he then anointed it. He gave it a blessing. That is a strange story, strangely told. He called it the House of God. So guess where Baal was supposed to live. In the stone. And every farmer had one at the end of the field...See how easy it was for Israel to move back and forth with stories like that? Baalism was fairly close to Jehovah worship in some respects. That confused the people. If they didn't have the spirit, they could lose the way easily. He also called the place the "gateway to heaven" and said that if you want to come to heaven, you have to come to the stone, or the house of God; so when he leaves, you can't get into heaven unless you come to the place he calls the gateway to heaven. What is another name for House of God? Temple. So the first temple constructed with any degree of permanence is a Rock which represents the experience that he had in the place. And the experience is where he sees the Atonement of Christ as it takes us from the telestial, to the terrestrial, all the way into the Presence of God in the celestial. The only way to get that is by the covenant made in the place called the House of the Lord, or the House of God, or the Temple. With that stone...and this is the first time the "stone" is introduced in the scriptures in the typification context, as a Temple, Jacob sees angels ascending and descending. You go all the way through the rest of the Old Testament without even a hint of the interpretation of that. You have to get to John 1:51, where Jesus is talking to Nathanael. 50 Jesus answered and said unto him, Because I said unto thee, I saw thee under the fig tree believest thou? thou shalt see greater things than these. 51 And he saith unto him, verily, verily, I say unto you, hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man. So WHO IS THE STONE? HIS ANGELS ASCEND AND DESCEND UPON THE SON OF MAN;JESUS CHRIST! WHO IS AT THE HEART OF ALL COVENANTS? THE SAME ONE WHO IS THE CARCASS! But now we have something else we need to deal with. The stone of Israel is now Christ. Therefore the temple is simply covenants that you make because of him. When the Lord finished the Sermon of the Mount, in which he told us to be perfect even as Father in Heaven is perfect, he that "heareth these things and doeth them is like him who is built upon A ROCK, so that when the winds blow and the waves crash, he is left standing." Guess where he is suggesting that these covenants are ultimately made? In the temple. In the STONE. He is the Stone of Israel; he went into the Temple built to his name; he cleaned the "outer court" a couple of times. The last week of his life was difficult. He knew they were going to kill him. Who is the cornerstone of the temple. He is. Therefore, what will happen if you pull out the corner-stone of the building. It will fall. Who are they ready to reject? The cornerstone (Jacob 4). He cleanses it, walks out of it and says not one stone will be left standing upon this place.

JACOB'S LADDER Genesis 28, another story, strangely told. This scene is critical. Jacob is fleeing for his life; he just stole the birthright from Esau, by gluing hair all over him, and deceiving his father for the blessing. Esau wants to kill him. Just getting the birthright seems strange. How can that kind of man be a prophet? If you were an Anti, like the anti-mormons who find fault with Joseph Smith, just look at Jacob and his family. Isn't there a double standard going on? Can you say that deceit and fraud and theft were OK thousands of years ago, and then say that Joseph's shortcomings prove he isn't a prophet. Can you imagine if the anti's lived in that time, if they would have followed Jacob! Absolutely not. They would have seen everything wrong with him. Theft from father-in-law, murder by children, incest, etc. But watch what happens to him when he leaves. 10 And Jacob went out from Beersheba, and went toward Haran. Beersheba means "seven wells" or "seven oaths" and went to Haran. 11 And he lighted upon a certain place, and tarried there all night, because the sun was set; and he took of the stones of that place and put them for his pillows, and lay down in that place to sleep. 12 And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set upon the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it. 13 And behold, the LORD stood above it, and said, I am the LORD God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac: and the land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed; 14 And thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth, and thou shalt spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north and to the south; and in thee and in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed. What does that sound like? The same thing given to Abraham and Isaac. What place are you obviously in? A temple. That is where covenants are made. 15 Behold, I am with thee and will keep thee in all places wither thou goest, and will bring thee again into this land; for I will not leave thee, until I have done that which I have spoken to thee of. 16 And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said, Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not. 17 And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.

There is a marvelous account that concerns Jacob and his marriage, as good an illustration as we have of how a strong-minded, faithful woman can influence a righteous husband to do the proper thing. I look upon Rebekah as one of the strongest characters mentioned in the whole body of revealed writ. In the account, Rebekah said to Isaac: "I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth: If Jacob take a wife of the daughters of Heth, such as these which are of the daughters of the land, what good shall my life do me?" Esau, Jacob's twin, had just done that very thing. So Rebekah in effect said that if Jacob were to marry out of the Church as Esau did, if he were to take to wife a daughter of the land, one of these nonmembers of the Church, what is her life worth? 'What is there left for me if my other son forsakes the gospel covenant and marries a nonmember of the Church?' In this way Rebekah stirred Jacob up. The account says: "And Isaac called Jacob, and blessed him, and charged him, and said unto him, Thou shalt not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan." That is to say: 'Thou shalt not marry out of the Church. My father, Abraham, said that in my seed and continuing in yours the blessings would come.'

quotes.text: Who did they just reject? The cornerstone. You kill me, the temple will also go with me. The Temple will come down and not one stone will be left upon another. So who is the stone of Israel? Christ. What is he representing? The Temple, and the right and power to make covenants. Where the carcass is, there will the eagles be gathered together. When you read the Psalms, and see the "Lord is my rock" or my stone, what is he? Where is his name, and where do you go to find him? Always the same place. In the house of the Lord, Beth-el, House of God. Mountain of the Lord's House. Peter said it; you are a royal priesthood, become "lively stones." Get it? The "lively stone" it Christ, and it represents the Temple,and all the covenants in it. There are two stones in the scriptures. Dead stones and lively stones. You make the covenants, you go into the temple and come out a "lively stone, with a name and a royal priesthood." It is all oriented to the temple. It is everywhere from the Garden of Eden to the Book of Revelation, but in cryptic language, only there for those with the spirit, and eye to see. The firm foundation is the temple.

quotes.text: In polygynous marriages, all of the firstborn sons of the various wives would be considered as the new leader before any of the secondborn or other sons. Only in monogamous marriages would the secondborn son be immediately considered as the potential new leader if the firstborn son proved unworthy. The Bible is not exactly clear as to why Jacob (the secondborn son) succeeded Esau (the firstborn son) as the head of Isaac's family, although it does mention that Isaac and Rebekah were sorely displeased and of "a grief of mind" because Esau had married wives of the Hittites (Gen. 26:34-35). Isaac also specifically forbade Jacob to "take a wife of the daughters of Canaan" (Gen. 28:1), and Rebekah lamented "if Jacob take a wife of the daughters of Heth, such as these which are of the daughters of the land, what good shall my life do me?" (Gen. 27:46.) Evidently the poor marriage choices of Esau disqualified him as the new leader of the house of Isaac, as well as the selling of his birthright for a mess of pottage. (Gen. 25:29-34.)
